Name: Francisco Mercado Rizal II
EARLY LIFE:
Francisco Rizal was only eight years old when his father died. After his father’s death, he was raised 
by his mother, Cirila Alejandro. Despite losing his father at a young age, Francisco received an 
education, while studying he met and fell in love with Teodora Alonso, a student in the 
College of Santa Rosa. Married on June 28, 1848. they settled down in Calamba where 
they were granted lease of a rice farm in the Dominican-owned haciendas.
PERSONALITY: He was an independent-minded, serious, taciturn, but dynamic gentleman
OCCUPATION:
Francisco Mercado Rizal II (often referred to as Don Francisco Engracio Rizal Mercado), 
the father of the Philippine national hero Jose Rizal, was primarily 
a prosperous farmer of sugarcane, rice, and other crops, agricultural businessman, and tenant

he also served as a local official or cabeza de barangay 
(barangay captain) in Calamba Laguna
INTERACTION WITH RIZAL: he was the role model, early guiding influence and the father of the national hero, Jose Rizal.
EDUCATIONAL BACKGROUND:
He attended a Latin school in Biñan, 
He also attended the Colegio de San Jose in Manila,
where he studied Latin and philosophy.
HOW THEY DIED:
Deep Grief and Old Age 

Local historical accounts note that he experienced 
a rapid physical decline due to heartbreak a year
later after the execution of his son, Jose Rizal
DATE OF DEATH:
died on January 5,1898, 
more than a year after
the execution of his son José.

Name: Teodora Alonso Realonda
EARLY LIFE: She came from a well educated family and later studied at Colegio de Santa Rosa in Intramuros where she received a good education. In 1848 She married Francisco Mercado ( Father of Rizal ) and moved to Calamba Laguna
PERSONALITY: Educated, disciplined, hardworking, and loving mother
INTERACTION WITH RIZAL: Teodora Alonso and Jose Rizal had a loving mother-and-son relationship. She was his first teacher, encouraged his talents, taught him values through stories, and inspired his fight against injustice. Rizal later repaid her kindness by caring for her as a physician.
EDUCATIONAL BACKGROUND: studied at Colegio de Santa Rosa in Intramuros

Name: Saturnina Rizal (Neneng)
EARLY LIFE: She was the eldest child and first daughter of Francisco Mercado Rizal and Teodora Alonso and a older sister of Jose Rizal. She helped take care of the younger Children in the family. Saturnina was also a well educated  and studied at the La Concordia College in Manila.
PERSONALITY: Responsible, caring, family-oriented, and supportive of her siblings.
OCCUPATION: Family member and supporter of José Rizal's literary works; later involved in publishing his works in Tagalog.
INTERACTION WITH RIZAL: She was José Rizal's eldest sister and remained one of the important members of his family.
EDUCATIONAL BACKGROUND: Saturnina Rizal studied at La Concordia College in Manila, where she received her education during her younger years.
HOW THEY DIED: Historical records do not clearly identify her specific cause of death.

Name: Paciano Rizal
EARLY LIFE: Paciano Rizal was born on March 9, 1851, in Calamba, Laguna. He was José Rizal's older brother and grew up in the Rizal family. He supported José's education and later became involved in the reform movement against Spanish colonial rule.
PERSONALITY: Radical, steadfast, and deeply patriotic a "revolutionary through and through." Unlike his younger brother who operated in the open, Paciano was quiet, preferred to operate "underground" and unseen, disliked being photographed (to the extent that his only surviving portrait was taken surreptitiously), and valued modesty and duty over prestige (he later declined a government position under the Americans).
OCCUPATION:
Revolutionary leader and military officer (Brigadier General in the Philippine Revolutionary Army; commander of Filipino forces in Laguna during the Philippine-American War).
Secretary of Finance in the Departmental Government of Central Luzon.
Katipunan director/member and propagandist/fundraiser for Diariong Tagalog.
Farmer in Laguna (after the revolution).
INTERACTION WITH RIZAL: Significant Contribution: Helped publish the Tagalog version of Noli Me Tangere in 1909, translated by Pascual H. Poblete
EDUCATIONAL BACKGROUND: The article specifically notes that he studied under and worked with Father José Burgos (one of the leaders of the Comité de Reformadores and the secularization movement), who served as his teacher, mentor, and friend.
HOW THEY DIED: He passed away due to tuberculosis in Los Baños, Laguna.

Name: Narcisa Rizal
EARLY LIFE: Narcisa married Antonino Manapat López, frequently called Antonio López, on 6 June 1875. He is commonly described in educational accounts as a teacher and musician from Morong. However, this description is repeated mainly in secondary biographies and instructional materials. It should not be presented as conclusively proven unless supported by an employment, parish, municipal or professional record.
DATE OF BIRTH: 29 October 1852, generally recorded in Calamba, Laguna
PERSONALITY: Narcisa Rizal was a loving, courageous, resourceful, loyal, and family-oriented woman who devotedly supported her brother José and preserved his memory.
OCCUPATION: Narcisa Rizal was primarily a homemaker and family caretaker; there is no strong historical evidence that she had a formal profession, while her husband, Antonio López, was reportedly a teacher and musician.
INTERACTION WITH RIZAL: Narcisa remained concerned for José during his imprisonment in Fort Santiago in 1896. Family accounts describe her as one of the relatives who attempted to maintain contact with him. José’s final communications demonstrate that he remained concerned about the safety and future of his family. His relatives, including Narcisa, faced the difficulty of visiting him under restrictions imposed by the Spanish colonial authorities.
EDUCATIONAL BACKGROUND: Narcisa Rizal’s formal educational background is not clearly documented, but she likely received basic home education in reading, writing, religion, and household management from her educated mother, Teodora Alonso.
HOW THEY DIED: She died on, during the Commonwealth period, at approximately 86 years old. Narcisa and several relatives were formerly buried at Manila North Cemetery. In 2013, reports documented the transfer of remains belonging to members of the Rizal family, including Narcisa, to Los Baños, Laguna.
DATE OF DEATH: She died on 24 June 1939, during the Commonwealth period, at approximately 86 years old.
SOURCE/LINK: National Historical Commission of the Philippines. Jose Rizal: Letters with Family Members. Manila: NHCP, 2011.,This is a 444-page government-published collection of primary correspondence. (library.nationalmuseum.gov.ph)

Name: Olympia Rizal
EARLY LIFE: Olympia Rizal Mercado (also spelled Olimpia) and also called in the nickname of Ypia / Ipia, She was the fourth child of Francisco Mercado and Teodora Alonso Realonda and one of José Rizal’s older sisters. Olimpia grew up in a large and prominent family together with her siblings in Calamba.
DATE OF BIRTH: she was born in December 1854 in Calamba, Laguna.
PERSONALITY: José Rizal affectionately teased Olimpia and referred to her as his “stout sister.” This suggests a playful and close sibling relationship. She was also trusted by José with personal matters concerning his first love.
OCCUPATION: Olimpia became the wife of Silvestre Ubaldo, a telegraph operator from Manila and had at least three sons. Historical sources do not clearly identify a separate profession for Olimpia herself.
INTERACTION WITH RIZAL: Olimpia was close to José. José confided in her about Segunda Katigbak, his first love. Since Segunda was Olimpia's schoolmate, Olimpia served as a mediator between José and Segunda. The one who corresponded with José while he was in Europe, giving him family news, including news about Saturnina's pregnancy and the cholera epidemic.
EDUCATIONAL BACKGROUND: She studied at La Concordia College in Manila, where she was a schoolmate of Segunda Katigbak.
HOW THEY DIED: Olimpia died from complications during childbirth, with some accounts specifically describing hemorrhage/bleeding while giving birth.
DATE OF DEATH: She died on September 22,1887 at the age of 32
SOURCE/LINK: Olimpia Rizal: the “Stout” sister of a hero. (2024, September 25). The Kahimyang Project. https://share.google/tAjmkeWMC9CovPOco

Name: Lucia Rizal
EARLY LIFE: Fifth child,  In 1889, Lucia’s husband Matriano Herbosa died during a cholera epidemic, a tragedy compounded by the refusal of the Catholic friars to grant him a Christian burial. The friars justified this denial by citing Mariano's connection to José Rizal, branding him as a “brother-in-law of a heretic.
PERSONALITY: Devoted mother, widow, and sister, she endured personal and political hardships while contributing to her brother José's educational and reformist efforts
OCCUPATION: She worked as a teacher, providing free education to women in Calamba, and actively participated in community and family welfare initiatives.
INTERACTION WITH RIZAL: She accompanied Jose when he returned to Manila in June the following year. She traveled to Dapitan to stay with José during his exile. She was present in his final days. After his execution she remained active, offering assistance to revolutionaries and sustaining the family’s networks through the turbulent years that followed.
EDUCATIONAL BACKGROUND: no reliable source of her educational background
HOW THEY DIED: Heart Disease and was buried in Manila North Cemetery, Manila, Philippines .
SOURCE/LINK: Lucía Rizal: Steadfast Sister in the Rizal Legacy

Name: Maria Rizal
EARLY LIFE: Maria Rizal is the sixth   child   Also called " Biang" As a child, Maria was part of a close-knit family living in a comfortable home in Calamba. The Rizals' affluence allowed their children access to education, a rarity for many Filipinos during the Spanish colonial era.
DATE OF BIRTH: was born in June 1859 in Calamba, Laguna (https://kahimyang.com/articles/3198/maria-rizal-the-brave-sister-who-stood-by-jose-rizal)
PERSONALITY: one of the closest, most trusted older sisters of the Philippine national hero, José Rizal , Though less celebrated than her brother, her role as a supportive sibling, confidante, and resilient woman offers a glimpse into the personal dynamics of the Rizal family and the broader historical context of the Philippines.
OCCUPATION: worked as a merchant and businesswoman, selling women's wear (sinamay) and dealing in copra.  (https://www.pressreader.com/philippines/manila-bulletin/20151208/281711203582718?srsltid=AfmBOooZpAYqDqfbEKBJKZNj4Mtkz0DMFeZIjRrBTuroF9fn6atcTIvC)
INTERACTION WITH RIZAL: Maria Rizal was a trusted confidante, supportive sister, and frequent letter recipient of her younger brother, Dr. José Rizal.  (https://kahimyang.com/articles/3198/The%20Hero's%20Confidant%20%7C%20OurHappySchool,%20%3Ca%20href=), [2] (https://www.studocu.com/ph/document/icct-colleges-foundation/criminology/chapter-3-the-rizal-mercado-family/97221769)
EDUCATIONAL BACKGROUND: was educated primarily at home during her early years. She came from a family that highly valued education, and their mother, Teodora Alonso, helped educate the children.
HOW THEY DIED: The exact cause of Maria Rizal’s death is not known because there are no reliable sources that clearly state what caused her death.
DATE OF DEATH: died on September 1, 1945, at the age of 86.  (https://ancestors.familysearch.org/en/KJ5H-PNV/maria-mercado-realonda-rizal-1859-1945)

Name: Concepcion Rizal
EARLY LIFE: Concepción Rizal, also known as “Concha,” was one of the children of Francisco Mercado Rizal and Teodora Alonso Realonda. She was the eighth child in the Rizal family and was born around 1862 in Calamba, Laguna. She was also the younger sister of José Rizal, who was born a year earlier in 1861. Concha grew up with her family in their home in Calamba. Sadly, she did not live for very long and died when she was only about three years old. Because of her young age and short life, there are not many records about her childhood, interests, or achievements.
PERSONALITY: There is not much reliable historical information about Concepción’s personality. However, stories about José Rizal’s childhood show that he was very close to his younger sister, Concha. They often played together and shared many childhood memories. Her death deeply affected José, especially since they had been close when they were young.
OCCUPATION: Concepción died when she was only about three years old. Since she was still very young, she did not have an occupation or profession.
INTERACTION WITH RIZAL: Concepción was very close to her older brother, José. Since they were only about a year apart, they spent a lot of time together when they were young. They played together and shared stories and other childhood memories. Concha’s death deeply affected José. According to stories about his childhood, her death was one of the first times he experienced deep sadness. José later remembered losing his little sister and described it as the first time he cried because of love and sorrow.
EDUCATIONAL BACKGROUND: There is no reliable record of Concepción Rizal having a formal education. This is not surprising since she died when she was only about three years old. She was too young to attend the formal schools that her older siblings later went to. Because of this, there is no known school that can be confirmed as part of her education.
HOW THEY DIED: Concepción Rizal died in 1865 from an illness when she was only about three years old.

Name: Josefa Rizal
EARLY LIFE: Josefa Rizal, the 9th child of the Rizal born in Calamba, Laguna, Philippines on 1865 also called 'Panggoy" family, Josefa broke the common view of women and the disabled. First  29 Female Members  of  KKK. She   became a  member of the  Katipunan  and  stood as President for the women's branch of the Katipunan. Although born with Epilepsy, it did not stop him from   helping   the   organization.   Josefa   became   proficient   in   speaking   English,   a   skill   which   was uncommon at that time and especially among women. She is probably the first handicapped individual to join the ranks of the revolution. She was given Nickname "Sumikat," for breaking both stereotype of woman and handicap. She was also Freemason convert espoused liberalismo through the 'Logia de Adopcion. https://www.studocu.com/ph/document/university-of-northern-philippines/life-and-works-of-rizal/rizals-family/93013812?sid=b60f128b-03c1-4662-af19-cc455a543ef51789276679
PERSONALITY: Josefa was known for her strong character, independence and dedication to educationhttps://www.scribd.com/document/936913673/Parent-and-Siblings-of-Jose-Rizal
OCCUPATION: She was a teacher and an advocate for womens rightshttps://www.scribd.com/document/936913673/Parent-and-Siblings-of-Jose-Rizal
INTERACTION WITH RIZAL: Among Jose’s letters to Josefa, the one dated October 26 1893 is perhaps the most fascinating. Written in English, the letter addressed Josefa as “Miss Josephine Rizal”, thereby making her the namesake of Rizal’s girlfriend Josephine Bracken. In the letter, Jose praised her sister for nearly mastering the English language, commenting that the only fault he found in Josefa’s letter is her apparent confusion between the terms ‘they are’ and ‘there’. Jose also wrote about the 20 pesos he sent, the 10 pesos of the amount was supposed for a lottery ticket. This indicates that Jose did not stop ‘investing’ in lottery tickets despite winning 6, 200 pesos in September the previous year. Even when he was in Madrid, he used to spend at least three pesetas monthly for his ‘only vice’https://www.studocu.com/ph/document/university-of-northern-philippines/life-and-works-of-rizal/rizals-family/93013812?sid=b60f128b-03c1-4662-af19-cc455a543ef51789276679

Name: Trinidad Rizal
EARLY LIFE:
Trinidad was born in Calamba, Laguna. She was the tenth child of Francisco Mercado Rizal and Teodora Alonso Realonda, making her one of José Rizal's younger sisters.

The eleven Rizal children, from eldest to youngest, were Saturnina, Paciano, Narcisa, Olimpia, Lucia, Maria, José, Concepcion, Josefa, Trinidad, and Soledad. Trinidad grew up in a relatively educated household, with Teodora playing an important role in the children's early education.
PERSONALITY: Trinidad Rizal can be characterized as courageous, compassionate, patriotic, discreet, and socially active. She joined the Katipunan, helped care for wounded revolutionaries, and participated in civic and women's organizations, which support these descriptions.
OCCUPATION: Trinidad doesn't have a clear occupation but she is described as a Revolutionary supporter, civic worker, and women's rights advocate.
INTERACTION WITH RIZAL: Trinidad Rizal had a close sibling relationship with José Rizal and supported him and his ideals. Their most historically significant interaction occurred shortly before José Rizal's execution in December 1896, when he told Trinidad that there was "something inside" a small alcohol stove given to the family. The hidden item was the manuscript of the poem later known as Mi Último Adiós.
EDUCATIONAL BACKGROUND: Trinidad Rizal's specific formal education is not clearly documented, although she grew up in the educated Rizal family under the influence of her mother, Teodora Alonso, who emphasized the importance of education.
HOW THEY DIED: Reliable historical sources, including the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP), do not specify the exact cause of her death.

Name: Soledad Rizal
EARLY LIFE: Soledad Rizal was the youngest of eleven children of Francisco Engracio Rizal Mercado and Teodora Alonso Realonda. She was born in 1870 in Calamba, Laguna. Her family called her “Choleng.” She grew up as the youngest sister of Dr. Jose Rizal, who later became the national hero of the Philippines. Although there is not much information about Soledad compared to her brother Jose, she grew up in a family that experienced many challenges. Her life also became connected to some controversies, especially regarding her choice of husband and later stories about her family and her parents.
DATE OF BIRTH: June 07, 1870. Born in: Calamba, Laguna, Philippines
PERSONALITY: Soledad Rizal married Pantaleón Quintero of Calamba on June 23, 1890, without parental consent. José Rizal criticized her decision because it affected family peace. She raised six children while balancing her family duties and community work.
OCCUPATION:
Pursued a career in teaching - a profession José deeply admired
In a June 6, 1890 letter, José advised her to be "a model of virtues and good qualities" for her students
INTERACTION WITH RIZAL: Soledad Rizal was one of José Rizal’s sisters. They had a close and loving relationship as siblings. She supported José and helped maintain their family while he was studying and fighting for the country.
EDUCATIONAL BACKGROUND: Among the best-educated of Rizal's sisters. Attended Colegio de la Concordia in Manila
HOW THEY DIED: She died of natural causes and spent her later years with her family in Calamba, Laguna.
